full_judgment:
7. Mr Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate, submits that the petitioner could not know about the disposal of the appeal and that his engaged Advocate could not appear in the final hearing, that is why he could not file the revisional application in time. He further submits that there is no prescribed period of limitation in filing revisional application, so application for condoning delay may be considered. 

 9. The submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that there is no prescribed period of limitation for filing a revisional application which can only be considered on a satisfactory and cogent explanation of delay caused in filing such an application. 

 "The Limitation Act does not provide for any period of limitation for an application in revision. The only Article which could be applicable was the residuary Article 181 which provides a limitation of 3(three) years for an application, but even that Article will not stand in the way of the exercise of revisional power for these powers can be exercised suo motu." 

 "The above observation is not to be understood to have laid down any law that Article 181 of the Limitation Act, 1908 governs an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It merely laid down emphasis on the principle that the High Court's power to revise an order suo motu is not restricted by any time limit." 

 14. The spirit of the above rulings is that High Court Division can condone delay in a suitable case where there is no negligence and laches on the part of the petitioner. This cardinal principle of our apex Court is very much in consonance with the spirit of the Limitation Act. The Limitation Act was enacted as far back as in 1908 with a view to putting an end to the litigation on the expiry of certain period prescribed therein. The necessity of such enactment lies in preventing the hazards which could be created in the face of claims raised after lapse of long time. The law of limitation puts an end to state claims once and for all. It debars that party from claiming rights after expiry of the period of limitation and can well be used in defence, otherwise the matter would be unending. 

 15. The accused-petitioner has filed this application for condo nation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act. Section 5 of the Limitation Act runs thus : 

 Section 5-Extension of period of certain cases-Any appeal or application for a revision or a review of judgment or for leave to appeal or any other application to which this may be made applicable by or under any enactment for the time being in force may be admitted after the period of limitation prescribed thereof, when the appellant or applicant satisfies the court that he had sufficient cause for not preferring appeal or making the application within such period. 

 Explanation:- The fact that the appellant or applicant was misled by any order, practice or judgment for the High Court Division in ascertaining or computing the prescribed period of limitation may be sufficient within the meaning of this section." 

 16. There is no prescribed period of limitation either in the Code of Criminal Procedure or in the Limitation Act for revision. There is a long practice being followed since the days of High Court Division that a revisional application is to be filed within the period of 90 days. But there is no legal bar to entertain, in the interest of justice, such revisional application even after the period of 90 (ninety) days provided the applicant can show that he was prevented by sufficient cause to move the High Court Division within the said period of 90 days. The revisional Court is to look into the question whether there has been gross negligence on the part of the petitioner or an inordinate delay in moving such revisional application. 

 19. Burden rests on the party who seeks indulgence of court in his favour to adduce distinct proof of sufficient cause on which he relies. It is for the accused-petitioner to show that his conduct throughout the period between the date of impugned judgment and filing of revision has been of such a character that it would be proper to condone the period of delay that has occurred beyond the period of limitation. The Court before exercising the powers under section 5 of the Limitation Act feels satisfied upon the facts of the case under consideration that the explanation given for the delay is sufficient. Where the condo nation is claimed on the ground that the accused-petitioner did not know of the order to be appealed against, in order to condone delay in filing a revisional application, the accused-petitioner must satisfy the Court as to the exact date when he came to know of the order appealed against and he must further explain the reasons for delay of every day after he came to know of it. Every day's delay must be properly explained. 

 21. In the instant case, laches caused in filing revisional application is intentional which was not beyond the control of the accused-petitioner. He was not prevented by sufficient cause. There was gross negligence on the part of the petitioner in filing the revisional application out of time. The accused-petitioner has totally failed to prove such long and inordinate delay. The statement made in the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act explaining the delay as aforesaid is vague and indefinite which cannot at all be considered satisfactory and cogent ground for condonation of delay. The explanations offered by the petitioner are unfounded and obscure which is a testimony of clear negligence and laches on his part in pursuing the proceedings instead of with due diligence and bonafide. The ground shown in the application for condo nation of delay as stated above does not give any opportunity to deviate from the aforesaid long standing settled practice of our apex Court in condoning such inordinate delay of 1710 days in making revisional application in this Court. The failure on the part of the petitioner to explain away the delay is a ground for refusing the prayer for condo nation of delay. The extension of time is thus a matter of concession of indulgence to the applicant and cannot be claimed by him as a matter of right. 

 22. A party wishing to take advantage of section 5 of the Limitation Act must satisfy the Court that it had not been negligent and had been prosecuting its case with due diligence and care. The petitioner is under a strict legal duty to furnish a reasonable explanation and to show sufficient cause for condo nation of inordinate delay.
